title: Search Open Technical Databases: WHOIS
summary: WHOIS is a public lookup service operated by registrars and the regional internet registries that allocate domain names and address blocks. A query returns the registration record for a domain or an address range: the registrant organisation, contact details, name servers, registrar identity, and creation and expiry dates. An adversary queries those records with a command line client or a web lookup page to map the domains a target owns, the providers that host them, and the mail infrastructure behind them. The activity is passive, because queries go to a third party registry rather than to the victim, so no victim-side log records the request. Defenders see it indirectly, through bulk lookup patterns from one source or through changes such as privacy shielding being removed from company domains. Legitimate research looks identical, so volume and correlation with later scanning separate the two.

beginner.definition: WHOIS is a public service that tells you who registered a domain name. It works like a phone book for websites. Anyone can look up a domain and read facts about the owner. People can also see the name servers and the creation date. This technique means an attacker reads those records before attacking.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your public domain records give away more than you expect. They can show your company name, your mail servers, and which company hosts your website. An attacker uses that to build a target list. The lookup never touches your network, so you will not see it in your own logs. This makes early warning much harder for your team.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a domain name that belongs to your company, such as the main website address.
They send a query to a WHOIS server run by a registrar or a regional internet registry.
The server replies with registration fields: owner, contacts, name servers, and date ranges.
The attacker repeats the query for related domains, IP blocks, and old versions of the record.
They combine the results with other public data to map your mail and hosting providers.
They keep the list and use it later for scanning or for phishing messages.
beginner.example: Think of a large office building with a public notice board in the lobby. The board lists the company name, the floor it rents, and the phone number of the reception desk. Anyone walking past can read it, and nobody writes down who looked. An attacker reads the board first and then decides which door to try. Your domain records are that notice board. The lookup is legal and quiet, which is exactly why it is popular.
takeaways: Public domain records are reconnaissance material, so keep them as small as your business allows.
You rarely see WHOIS lookups in your own logs because the queries go to a third party.
Watch for bulk lookups of many of your domains coming from a single source.

objectives: Explain what a WHOIS registration record contains and which organisations publish it.
Describe why a WHOIS lookup leaves no trace in the victim's own logging.
Identify the registration fields that an attacker finds most useful.
List defensive steps that reduce the amount of registration data you expose.
Recognise bulk or automated WHOIS querying as an early reconnaissance signal.
